facts.statement: The study used two mouse models of prolactinoma that do not involve the Men1 gene, where only female mice developed the tumors.
facts.subject: animals

facts.statement: The amount of Men1 gene in the pituitary glands did not change between the different mouse groups or sexes.
facts.subject: animals

facts.statement: In the tumor cells, the menin protein was found mostly in the cell body rather than in the nucleus.
facts.subject: animals

facts.statement: The absence of menin in the nucleus was linked to changes in several other proteins that control cell growth and survival.
facts.subject: animals

facts.statement: Treating the mice with dopamine-agonist drugs kept menin in the nucleus, while blocking dopamine or adding estradiol caused it to leave the nucleus.
facts.subject: animals

facts.statement: In human samples, menin was present in both the nucleus and cell body of pituitary cells from healthy individuals and from tumor patients who had received dopamine-agonist treatment.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: In one untreated female patient with a prolactinoma, the menin protein was less clearly visible in the nucleus compared to treated cases.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: The results suggest that sporadic prolactinomas have a functional lack of menin activity because the protein is kept out of the nucleus, which may be a target for new treatments.
facts.subject: other
